## Chapter 1

Drifting in the dead-water of the fin-de-siècle, where not a breath stirred the idle air of education, one lived alone. Adams had long ceased going into society; for years he had not dined out of his own house, and in public his face was as unknown as that of an extinct statesman. Six months' oblivion amounts to newspaper-death, and resurrection is rare. Nothing is easier, if a man wants it, than rest profound as the grave.

A few houses remained which he could enter without being asked, and quit without being noticed. One was Hay's; another Cabot Lodge's; a third led to intimacy with Senator Cameron of Pennsylvania, whose marriage in 1880 to a niece of Senator Sherman made an alliance of dynastic importance. For sixteen years Mrs. Cameron and Mrs. Lodge dispensed sunshine over Washington. Whatever one's politics, one's house was bound to the Republican interest, sandwiched between Cameron, Hay, and Lodge, with Theodore Roosevelt at home in them all.

In February, 1893, the Camerons took Adams to South Carolina; from there he went on to Havana, returned to linger till April, and in May went with them to Chicago to see the Exposition. In June all sailed for England, and by July they were in Switzerland.

Months of close contact teach character. The Cameron type had keen interest for Adams, ever since it had shipwrecked his career in President Grant. The Pennsylvania mind was not complex; it reasoned little and never talked; but in practical matters it was the steadiest of all American types. The true Pennsylvanian was as narrow as the kirk; to him, none but Pennsylvanians were white. Yet when he allied his interests, he became supple in action and large in motive.

Never had a Cameron believed in an Adams, or an Adams in a Cameron; but Pennsylvania had set up the Government in 1789, saved it in 1861, created the American system, developed its iron and coal, invented its great railways. Cameron's qualities and defects united to make him the most useful member of the Senate.

On the great subject of that year — silver — Cameron made deep impression. Adams had taken no interest, but inevitably, when forced to choose sides, was sure to choose silver. Every political idea and personal prejudice held him to it. One could not have a political and an economical policy at the same time; this was heresy in the English school but had always been law in the American. He admitted his interests lay wholly with gold; but masses of men invariably follow interests in deciding morals, and his last chance of standing up for his eighteenth-century principles — strict construction, limited powers, George Washington, John Adams — lay behind silver.

The case seemed entirely different with Cameron, the practical politician whom all the reformers had abused for a lifetime for subservience to moneyed interests. He stood out obstinately as the leading champion of silver in the East, and the reformers at once denounced his corruption.

Of all the lessons Adams learned from the banks, none compared in dramatic effect with that of July 22, 1893, when, after talking silver all morning with Senator Cameron crossing the Furka Pass, they reached Lucerne to find letters requesting his immediate return because the community was bankrupt and he was probably a beggar.

If he wanted education, he knew no quicker mode of learning a lesson than that of being struck on the head by it. By slow degrees the situation dawned on him that the banks had lent him money for which he was responsible and of which he knew no more than they. The humor seemed sharper than the terror. He had nothing to lose he cared about; the banks stood to lose their existence. When he went to draw a hundred dollars of his own deposit, the cashier refused him more than fifty; Adams accepted without complaint because he was himself refusing to let the banks have hundreds that belonged to them. Blindly some very powerful energy was at work, doing something nobody wanted done.

Men died like flies, and Boston grew old, haggard, thin. Adams alone waxed fat and was happy, for at last he had got hold of his world. Great changes had taken place since 1870 in the forces at work; the old machine ran behind its duty; somewhere it was bound to break down, and if it broke precisely over one's head, it gave the better chance for study.

His brother Brooks, working out a law of history that civilization followed the exchanges, had reached the paradox that, in the disequilibrium between capital and labor, the logical outcome was not collectivism but anarchism. Henry made note of it for study.

In September, the storm having partly blown over, Adams set off to Chicago to study the Exposition again. The Exposition itself defied philosophy. As a scenic display, Paris had never approached it, but the inconceivable thing was its being there at all — more surprising than Niagara or Yellowstone, since these were natural products in their place, while the Exposition was Babel raised on the shore of Lake Michigan. That it should be a natural growth of the Northwest offered a step in evolution to startle Darwin. The American had the air of enjoying it as though it were all his own; he had leaped from Corinth and Syracuse and Venice, over the heads of London and New York, to impose classical standards on plastic Chicago.

One sat down to ponder on the steps beneath Richard Hunt's dome almost as deeply as on the steps of Ara Cœli. Was the rupture real? If real, the new American world could take a sharp and conscious twist towards ideals.

For the historian alone the Exposition made a serious effort. The ocean steamer ran the surest line of triangulation into the future; the dynamo taught least because it had barely reached infancy, yet if its progress were constant, it would result in infinite costless energy within a generation. One lingered long among the dynamos. When the historian came on a new power, he asked naturally what it was — did it pull or push, was it a screw or thrust, did it flow or vibrate? — and got no answers.

Chicago asked in 1893 for the first time whether the American people knew where they were driving. Adams answered, for one, that he did not know. They probably knew no more than he; but they might still be driving or drifting unconsciously to some point in thought. Chicago was the first expression of American thought as a unity; one must start there.

Washington was the second. He fell headlong into the extra session called to repeal the Silver Act. He had stood up for his eighteenth century — his Constitution of 1789, his George Washington, his Harvard College, his Quincy, his Plymouth Pilgrims — as long as any one would stand up with him. He had hugged his antiquated dislike of bankers and capitalistic society until he had become little better than a crank. For a hundred years the American people had hesitated between two forces, one industrial, the other capitalistic. In 1893 the issue came on the single gold standard, and the majority at last declared itself in favor of the capitalistic system with all its necessary machinery.

The vote came; the gold standard won; and Adams, with his eighteenth-century prejudices, accepted that the capitalistic system had absorbed his class along with the rest, leaving only the question how long and how far its acceleration would run.

## Chapter 3

The convulsion of 1893 left its victims in dead-water and closed much education. Among the earliest wreckage had been the fortunes of Clarence King. In 1871 Adams had thought King's education ideal — physical energy, social standing, mental scope, wit, geniality, and science combined. Twenty years' effort proved that the theory of scientific education failed where most theory fails — for want of money. Even Adams, who kept himself quite outside of every possible financial risk, had been caught in the cogs, saved only by the chance that the whole class of millionaires were bankrupt too. Education without capital could always be taken by the throat and forced to disgorge its gains.

In theory the scientific scheme alone was sound, for science should be equivalent to money; in practice science was helpless without money. Among Adams's contemporaries trained to professions, three were typical — John Hay, Whitelaw Reid, William C. Whitney — all of whom owed their free hand to marriage, education serving only for ornament. By 1893 Whitney had finished with politics after gratifying every ambition; he had thrown away the usual objects of political ambition like the ashes of smoked cigarettes, satiated every taste, and carried his field of activity abroad. He had succeeded precisely where Clarence King had failed.

One knew no better in 1894 than in 1854 what an American education ought to be in order to count as success. A mathematician, linguist, chemist, electrician, engineer, if fortunate, might average ten dollars a day; an administrator with mediæval qualities of energy and will, but no education beyond his special branch, would probably be worth ten times as much. Society had failed to discover what sort of education suited it best.

King's breakdown brought the indirect gain that he induced Adams to go to Cuba, where in January, 1894, they drifted into Santiago. The picturesque Cuban society made no profession of teaching anything unless it were Spanish; but the decaying fabric fell on their heads. The Cuban rebellion severed the last tie that attached Adams to a Democratic administration; he thought Cleveland could have settled the question without war, had he chosen to do his duty. The new American had turned his back on the nineteenth century before he was done with it; the gold standard, the protective system, and the laws of mass could have no other outcome.

After passing the winter with King in the West Indies and the summer with Hay in the Yellowstone, Adams set out for Mexico and the Gulf with desperate thirst for exhausting the American field, clearing up some twenty thousand miles of American land and water.

By April, 1895, he thought he knew enough about the edges of life — tropical islands, mountain solitudes, archaic law, retrograde types. They educated only artists, and as one's sixtieth year approached the artist began to die. Taking for granted that the alternative to art was arithmetic, he plunged into statistics. The Government volunteered endless columns of figures merely for the asking. Yet the statisticians showed no enthusiastic confidence in their own figures; the method did not result in faith. Every increase of mass seemed to bring in new elements, and at last a scholar fresh in arithmetic fell into a superstitious terror of complexity. These societies, violating every law moral, arithmetical, and economical, propagated each other.

The human factor was worse. No one seemed concerned about this world or the future, unless it were the anarchists, and they only because they disliked the present. Since 1850 massacres had become so common that society scarcely noticed them unless they summed up hundreds of thousands; wars had been almost continuous. The robbery might be natural and inevitable, but the murder seemed altogether archaic. He took to study of the religious press for signs of growth in human nature; he very gravely doubted, from his aching consciousness of religious void, whether any large fraction of society cared for a future life, or even for the present one, thirty years hence.

For the moment he was rescued, as often before, by a woman. Towards midsummer, 1895, Mrs. Cabot Lodge bade him follow her to Europe. So it chanced that in August one found one's self for the first time at Caen, Coutances, and Mont-Saint-Michel in Normandy. If history had a chapter with which he thought himself familiar, it was the twelfth and thirteenth centuries; yet these bare playgrounds of the lecture system turned into green and verdurous virgin forests merely through the medium of younger eyes. His German bias must have given his youth a terrible twist, for the Lodges saw at a glance what he had thought unessential because un-German. They breathed native air in the Normandy of 1200. The old problem became new and personal; it expelled archaic law and antiquarianism once for all, and Adams drifted back to Washington with a new sense of history.

After covering once more many thousand miles of the old trails, Adams went home in October, 1896, to elect McKinley President and start the world anew. Suddenly Mr. McKinley entered the White House and laid his hand heavily on his special group. In a moment the whole nest, slowly constructed, was torn to pieces and scattered over the world. John Hay took his orders for London; Rockhill departed to Athens; Spring-Rice had been buried in Persia; Cameron broke up his house. Adams found himself alone. To one whose interests lay chiefly in foreign affairs, the man in the State Department seemed more important than the man in the White House; yet the President meant to put Senator John Sherman in the State Department to make a place for Mr. Hanna — Sherman notoriously feeble and senile, the intrigue the betrayal of an old friend. One could bear coldly the jobbery of enemies, but not that of friends.

In every society worth the name, the man of sixty had been encouraged to ride his hobby — the Pursuit of Ignorance in Silence — as though it were the easiest way to get rid of him. "Even a fool," said the wisest of men, "when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise"; and Vigny's dying wolf affirmed: "Only silence is strong; all the rest is but lies." Once more, one must go.

He arrived in London on April 21, 1897, where Hay was to be established. Carlton House Terrace squeaked and gibbered with ghosts till one felt like Odysseus before the press of shadows; but in spring London is pleasant. He soon found himself the oldest Englishman in England, and slipped away to Paris, where he set up a household at St. Germain. He lingered there till the Hays came by in January, 1898, and Mrs. Hay bade him go with them to Egypt.

Adams cared little to see Egypt again, but was glad to see Hay, and readily drifted after him to the Nile. What they saw had as little to do with education as possible, until one evening, as they looked at the sun set across the Nile from Assouan, a telegram announced the sinking of the Maine in Havana Harbor. This was the greatest stride in education since 1865, but what did it teach? One leant on a fragment of column at Karnak and watched a jackal creep down the débris of ruin. The jackal's ancestors had surely crept up the same wall when it was building. What was his view about the value of silence? One lay in the sands and watched the expression of the Sphinx. Brooks Adams had taught him that the relation between civilizations was that of trade. Henry wandered, or was storm-driven, down the coast — Ephesus, Athens, Tiryns, Constantinople with its great walls and greater domes. His hobby had turned into a camel, and he hoped, if he rode long enough in silence, that at last he might come on a city of thought along the great highways of exchange.
